slides.title: Evolution of ASR

visualInspection.notes: Timeline figure: FFT algorithms in the 1960–70s; statistical HMM–GMM ASR in the 1990s; hybrid neural-HMM alternatives in the 2000s; RNN/LSTM deep-learning ASR around 2010; CTC and RNN-Transducer end-to-end ASR in the mid-2010s; attention, encoder-decoder, and Transformers at the source’s present. Treat eras as a simplified source timeline, not exact invention dates or a claim about the current state of the art. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: What is Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR)

visualInspection.notes: ASR/STT maps acoustic speech to words or discrete text tokens. It is distinct from semantic interpretation and TTS. The waveform-to-text figure says “It’s time for lunch!” Modern systems may support language identification, translation, and speech-activity decisions, but multitask support does not imply every task is performed simultaneously on every call. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: How do robots understand speech?

visualInspection.notes: Microphone converts acoustic pressure into an analog electrical signal; the diagram orders speech, microphone/waveform, ASR, text, language understanding, and robot action. The analog voltage exactly mimics the acoustic shape only as an idealization of a real microphone transfer function. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Visualizing Speech as an Acoustic Waveform

visualInspection.notes: Waveform axes are amplitude versus time, with a short approximately periodic segment from 0 to 0.03875 seconds. Amplitude relates to loudness under otherwise comparable conditions; repetition frequency relates to pitch, not a universal single-frequency description of all speech. Speech begins as varying air pressure and must be digitized for the illustrated processing. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Stages in Speech Feature Extraction                                                                 DFT: Discrete Fourier

visualInspection.notes: Feature pipeline figure: digitization, windowing/framing, DFT, log-Mel spectrum, then MFCC. Acronyms DFT and MFCC expanded. Output is a sequence of acoustic feature vectors. Whisper uses log-Mel input rather than requiring the final MFCC/DCT step; the entire pictured chain is not mandatory for every ASR model. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Stage 1: Digitization

visualInspection.notes: Digitization is sampling followed by quantization. Sampling gives discrete times at a rate such as 16 kHz; quantization maps measured amplitudes to finite levels, illustrated by 8- or 16-bit integers. Sampling alone does not quantize amplitude. Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate; a bandlimited signal and boundary/phase conditions are needed for accurate reconstruction, not the unqualified at-least-twice slogan. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Stage 2: Windowing/Framing

visualInspection.notes: Speech is nonstationary but short frames are treated as approximately stationary. The three window parameters are size, stride, and shape. Multiplication y[n] = w[n]s[n] selects and weights samples; it is not convolution. Window length and stride are different, allowing overlap. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Stage 2: Windowing/Framing (contd.)

visualInspection.notes: Rectangular and Hamming equations and both waveform plots inspected. The printed Hamming formula is 0.54 − 0.46 cos(2πn/L), 0 ≤ n ≤ L−1: a periodic convention, unlike symmetric denominator L−1. The claim that Hamming reaches zero at its boundaries is false: w[0] = 0.08. The prose calls L a number of frames although the formula indexes samples. Smooth curves illustrate already discrete sampled inputs. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Stage 3: Frequency Analysis

visualInspection.notes: DFT equation X[k] = Σ x[n] exp(−j2πkn/N), n from 0 to N−1, and waveform-to-spectrum figure inspected. DFT gives complex magnitude/phase coefficients; FFT is an efficient algorithm for the same transform. The source uses a 25 ms Hamming-windowed frame and a frequency axis to 8000 Hz. Magnitude/power and dB scaling are later representations rather than the raw complex DFT itself. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Stage 4: Mel Filter Bank & Log Spectrum

visualInspection.notes: Overlapping triangular Mel filters are narrower and more closely spaced at low physical frequencies, wider at high frequencies. Their energy outputs form the Mel spectrum. The displayed convention is mel(f) = 1127 ln(1 + f/700), with f in Hz. This is one Mel convention, not all library defaults. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Stage 4: Mel Filter Bank & Log Spectrum (contd.)

visualInspection.notes: Each filter yields one scalar channel energy; the vector contains M channels. Logarithm is applied elementwise. The notation m_i refers ambiguously to filter and output energy; distinguish the weighted filter from its scalar response. Actual Whisper preprocessing also includes implementation-specific clamping, scaling, and feature-count conventions, so the generic log vector alone is not the exact numerical implementation. slides.title: Stage 5: Extracting MFCCs (Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients)

visualInspection.notes: MFCCs capture a compact spectral-envelope/vocal-tract representation. A cepstrum plot shows amplitude against sample index. Overall energy and dynamic features are named, but these depend on whether energy and temporal delta features are included; a single static MFCC vector does not automatically contain temporal derivatives. Whisper uses log-Mel features instead of requiring MFCCs. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Traditional ASR pipeline

visualInspection.notes: Traditional ASR: acoustic HMM–GMM model, pronunciation lexicon mapping words to phonemes, language model, and search decoder. The claim that every component is independently trained is too broad: a lexicon may be curated and a decoder is a search algorithm. End-to-end networks can combine modeling roles, but do not eliminate all preprocessing, search, or optional language-model integration. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Limitations of Traditional Systems

visualInspection.notes: Sequence mismatch example: features every 10 ms, acoustic sequence 5 to 19 times text length. The ratio depends on tokenization, duration, and speech rate and is not universal. The Venn diagram places ASR at machine learning, signal processing, and NLP. Subsampling reduces length but alone does not solve variable speech/text alignment. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

visualInspection.notes: One-frame temporal CNN illustration: z_j = x_j w_0 for 1 ≤ j ≤ t, with local dot products. The stride-one same-length statement is true for this one-frame case or suitable padding, not arbitrary valid convolutions. The scalar equation suppresses vector/channel dimensions. slides.title: CNNs for Speech Recognition

visualInspection.notes: Odd-width kernel equation z_j = Σ from i=−p to p of x_(j+i) w_(i+p). Here p acts as half-width; equal zero padding can preserve length at stride one. Diagram shows padded edges and a three-weight kernel. A second equation sums channel convolutions but suppresses distinct per-channel weights and output channels. Stride greater than one reduces temporal length but need not skip every sample contribution or by itself solve alignment. Deep-learning Conv1d generally implements cross-correlation rather than weight-reversed mathematical convolution. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Transformer-Based Speech Recognition

visualInspection.notes: Encoder-decoder diagram: 80-dimensional log-Mel frames, subsampling into shorter sequence X, encoder contextual output H, decoder receiving a start symbol and shifted previous text to predict “it’s time…”. Encoder listens and decoder generates one character or subword token at a time. This is the architecture shown, not a requirement for all ASR systems. slides.title: Transformer-Based Speech Recognition

visualInspection.notes: Cross-attention uses Q from decoder hidden states and K,V from encoder acoustic representations. Equations Q=H_dec WQ, K=H_enc WK, V=H_enc WV and softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V inspected. Diagram includes encoder self-attention, decoder causal self-attention, decoder cross-attention, normalization, feedforward layers, residual paths, and a language-modeling output head. Cross-attention is standard in encoder-decoder Transformers, not a new addition unique to speech. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Transformer-Based Speech Recognition

visualInspection.notes: Causal decoder self-attention uses prior text, unlike acoustic cross-attention. Greedy decoding selects the highest conditional next-token probability and feeds that token back. The source uses characters as an illustration; modern tokenizers may use subwords. Local greedy choices do not guarantee the highest joint sequence probability. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Transformer-Based Speech Recognition

visualInspection.notes: Autoregressive product conditions every term on audio and earlier tokens, although the displayed left side omits the conditioning on X. Scoring is literally log P(Y|X)/|Y|_c + λ log P_LM(Y): only the acoustic term is length-normalized, not the whole sum. External LM influence is controlled by λ. This is an example scoring rule, not proof that default Whisper decoding uses external LM fusion. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Whisper                                          •  Audio is converted into a 128-channel

visualInspection.notes: Whisper diagram labels sinusoidal position encoding on the audio encoder and learned positional encoding on the text decoder. The prose incorrectly calls audio positions learned. The blanket 128-channel feature claim needs a model/version qualification: the following code names whisper-small. Two Conv1D+GELU stages precede the encoder, and cross-attention connects encoder to autoregressive decoder. Task/language/timestamp and start tokens are drawn; multilingual task support is not necessarily simultaneous output of every task. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: Applications of ASR

visualInspection.notes: Applications: robot conversational command transcription, human-computer interfaces, media captions, and accessibility for difficulty typing or hearing. Text output is an input to interpretation, not sufficient semantic understanding or safe robot execution by itself. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

slides.title: What happens after ASR?

visualInspection.notes: Post-ASR pipeline: text transcription, language understanding/response generation, then text-to-speech. An LLM is the source’s example implementation, not the only possible NLU method. TTS reverses the input/output modality direction but is not a mathematical inverse recovering the original speaker/prosody. Speech-to-speech models may use discrete acoustic tokens to bypass an explicit text transcript. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.
